name: Strategy / Management
description: A simulation the player steers from above. The interface is usually the biggest area, since the player reads the game through it.

pillars.name: Watch It Grow
pillars.feeling: the satisfaction of a system I built running on its own

pillars.name: Information at a Glance
pillars.feeling: I can see why things happen

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A colony builder where the player grows a settlement from a camp to a city by balancing production chains.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Survey resources.
2. Place buildings and assign workers.
3. Watch the simulation run and spot bottlenecks.
4. Expand and upgrade.

gameExamples.heading: Non-goals
gameExamples.text:
- Direct unit combat.
- Real-time twitch input.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.summary: The rules that run the world underneath the player.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: The simulation runs on a fixed tick separate from frame rate. Systems update in a fixed order each tick, so results are deterministic.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USimulationSubsystem`: runs the tick and system order
- `ISimulationSystem`: interface each system implements

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Tick rate and system order in a data asset.

docs.title: Resources
docs.summary: What exists to be gathered, stored and spent.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Resources are typed amounts stored in stockpiles. Buildings request and deliver resources through the stockpile system.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UResourceDefinition`: data asset per resource
- `UStockpileComponent`: stores and reserves resources

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Resource definitions as data assets.
- Stockpile capacities per building.

docs.title: Production Chains
docs.summary: How resources turn into other resources.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Each production building has recipes: inputs, outputs and a time. Buildings pull inputs from the nearest stockpile and push outputs back.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProductionComponent`: runs recipes
- `URecipeDefinition`: inputs, outputs and time

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Recipes as data assets.
- Production times in simulation ticks.

docs.title: Time and Tick
docs.summary: Simulation speed, pausing and keeping it deterministic and fast.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Game speed scales how many simulation ticks run per second. Pausing stops ticks but not the UI.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text: - `USimulationClock`: speed, pause and tick counter

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Speed steps (1x, 2x, 4x).

docs.title: Units
docs.summary: The things that act in the world, and what the player can tell them to do.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can select units and give them orders.
- As a player, I can assign workers to buildings.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Selection circles and order markers.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Workers walk to their job.
- Idle units are highlighted.

docs.title: Unit AI
docs.summary: How units decide what to do.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Units pick jobs from a job board by priority and distance. Each job is a small state machine (walk, work, deliver).

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UJobBoardSubsystem`: posts and assigns jobs
- `UUnitBrainComponent`: picks and runs jobs

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Job priorities in a data asset.

docs.title: Pathfinding
docs.summary: How units move across the map at scale.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Units use a flow field per destination on a grid, so hundreds of units can share one path calculation.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text: - `UFlowFieldSubsystem`: builds and caches flow fields

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Grid cell size and update budget.

docs.title: Unit Assets
docs.summary: Unit meshes, animations and selection sounds.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Worker meshes | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Work animations | Animation | Placeholder | To source |
| Selection sounds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Small, readable figures: color identifies the job, silhouette identifies the unit type.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Low-poly character packs with work animations.
- Packs designed for top-down cameras.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Highly detailed characters that become noise when zoomed out.

docs.title: Building
docs.summary: Placing, connecting and upgrading structures.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can place structures where I want.
- As a player, I can see if a placement is valid before confirming.
- As a player, I can upgrade or remove what I built.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A ghost preview, green when valid and red when not.
- Costs shown before placing.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Structures snap to a grid.
- Removing returns part of the cost.

docs.title: Placement Code
docs.summary: Grid or free placement, validation and connections.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Buildings snap to a grid; placement checks the footprint against terrain, other buildings and resources before confirming.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UPlacementSubsystem`: ghost previews and validation
- `UBuildingFootprint`: grid cells a building covers

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Footprints per building data asset.

docs.title: Building Assets
docs.summary: Building meshes for each stage, and construction effects.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Building meshes per tier | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Construction scaffolding | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Smoke and work effects | VFX | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Each building type has a unique roof shape so it's recognizable from far above.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Building packs with several upgrade stages.
- Packs designed for top-down views.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Buildings that all share one silhouette.

docs.title: Economy and Balancing
docs.summary: Costs, rates and tuning that keep choices meaningful.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can make trade-offs between growth and stability.
- As a player, I can see where resources go.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Graphs of income and spending.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- No resource is ever useless.
- Every building has an upkeep.

docs.title: Camera and Controls
docs.summary: How the player views the map and selects and commands things.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A top-down pawn moves with edge scroll, keys and drag; zoom changes height and angle together.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `AStrategyCameraPawn`: pan, zoom and rotate
- `USelectionComponent`: box and click selection

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Zoom levels and pan speeds in a data asset.

docs.title: Map
docs.summary: Hand-made or generated maps, terrain and resource placement.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start on a new map each game.
- As a player, I can read terrain and resources at a glance.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Resources visible on the terrain.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Every map has enough starting resources nearby.

docs.title: Map Generation
docs.summary: Generating terrain and placing resources.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Maps are generated from a seed: noise for terrain, then rules place resources and the starting area.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text: - `UMapGenerator`: terrain and resource placement

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Generation settings per map size.

docs.title: Terrain Art
docs.summary: Terrain materials, foliage and resource node meshes.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Terrain materials | Material | Placeholder | To source |
| Trees and foliage | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Resource node meshes | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Soft, readable terrain with resources in strong, distinct colors.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Stylized landscape material packs.
- Foliage packs that stay readable from above.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Realistic grass that hides resources.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.title: UI Art
docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Fonts (headings, body) | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Panel and button skins | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Input prompt icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.summary: Map overlays that show simulation data.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text: - As a player, I can toggle overlays for happiness, resources and traffic.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Color-coded heatmaps on the map.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Only one overlay at a time.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.summary: Alerts that pull the player's attention to what matters.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can get alerts about problems.
- As a player, I can jump to the problem from the alert.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A notification feed in the corner.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Repeated alerts are grouped.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.
